name: Pang Lhabsol
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month (lunar)
community: Bhutia and Lepcha, with all Sikkimese communities
summary: Pang Lhabsol is the festival at which Sikkim honours Kangchenjunga as its guardian deity and remembers the blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. In Gangtok, monks perform masked dances, including a warrior dance, at the Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel.
body: Kangchenjunga is not only a mountain in Sikkim. Sikkim's Buddhists worship it as Dzö-nga, the guardian deity of the land, and Pang Lhabsol is its festival, held on the 15th day of the 7th month of the Tibetan calendar, which falls in August or September. It also commemorates the oath of blood brotherhood that, in Sikkimese tradition, the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa swore at Kabi Lungchok in the 13th century, with the mountain as witness. Wikipedia's article on Enchey Monastery describes Pang Lhabsol in these terms.

In Gangtok the main celebration takes place in the courtyard of the Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel in the old palace compound near the centre of town. Monks in masks and brocade perform chaam dances honouring the mountain deity and its attendants, and a warrior dance recalls the kingdom's armed protectors. Families in traditional dress fill the courtyard, and the day is a state holiday in Sikkim.

Pang Lhabsol is also marked at other monasteries, including Enchey, and at Ravangla in South Sikkim. The dates follow the lunar calendar and change every year. The monsoon is often still active, so roads can be slow; plan Gangtok-based days around it and check current status before you travel.
tips: Reach the Tsuklakhang courtyard early for a place to stand or sit; it fills by mid-morning.
Carry an umbrella or raincoat, since Pang Lhabsol often falls in the last weeks of the monsoon.
Do not step into the dance area, and use no flash when photographing the dancers.

faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, usually in late August or September. The Gregorian date changes each year and is fixed by the lunar calendar; Sikkim's government holiday list gives it once announced. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for the confirmed date.

faqs.q: Where can we watch Pang Lhabsol in Gangtok?
faqs.a: The main masked dances in Gangtok take place in the courtyard of the Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel in the palace compound near the centre of town. Other monasteries, including Enchey, also mark the day. Access arrangements vary each year, so arrive early and follow instructions from organisers and police.

It honours Kangchenjunga, worshipped in Sikkim as the guardian deity Dzö-nga, and commemorates the blood-brotherhood oath between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples sworn at Kabi Lungchok in the 13th century, according to Sikkimese tradition. It is one of the most distinctly Sikkimese festivals and a state holiday.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Gangtok for Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: It can be, if you accept monsoon conditions. Gangtok itself is usually accessible, but NH10 from Siliguri closes after landslides at times, and mountain views are rare. Keep a buffer day, plan on the Kalimpong or Algarah route if NH10 is shut, and check current status before you travel.

name: Losoong and the Kagyed dance
when: December; Kagyed on the 28th–29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, Losoong a few days later (lunar)
community: Bhutia, with Lepcha Namsoong in the same season
summary: Losoong is the Sikkimese Bhutia new year and harvest festival, held in December. In Gangtok it is preceded by the Kagyed dance at the Tsuklakhang, performed by monks of Pemayangtse on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month to clear away the old year's obstacles.
body: Losoong marks the end of the harvest and the turn of the year for Sikkim's Bhutia community, and Wikipedia notes that it is celebrated every December. The Lepcha celebrate Namsoong in the same season, so the state holiday is usually listed as Losoong/Namsoong. For families it is a time for new clothes, visits to relatives, special food and offerings at home and at the monasteries.

The public highlight in Gangtok comes first. On the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, usually early December, monks from Pemayangtse Monastery perform the Kagyed dance in the shrine hall courtyard of the Tsuklakhang Palace, according to Wikipedia's article on Kagyed. Masked dancers representing protector deities destroy effigies of evil, and jesters provide comic relief between the solemn dances. Similar dances are held at Rumtek and Phodong.

Losoong follows a few days later. Dates are fixed by the lunar calendar, so they move each year; we confirm them in November. December is dry and clear in Gangtok, with cold mornings and good mountain views, making this one of the best festival seasons to visit.
tips: Arrive at the Tsuklakhang by 9 am on Kagyed days; the courtyard is small and fills quickly.
Dress warmly: December mornings in Gangtok are around 5–8 °C.
Combine Losoong with a Dzongu homestay for the Lepcha Namsoong at Namprikdang.

faqs.a: Losoong falls in December, at the end of the harvest and the turn of the Sikkimese year. The Kagyed dance at the Tsuklakhang comes first, on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, usually early December. Exact dates change every year. Check current status before you travel.

Kagyed is a masked dance performed by monks to destroy the obstacles of the old year before Losoong. In Gangtok, monks from Pemayangtse perform it at the Tsuklakhang Palace on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, according to Wikipedia. Jesters appear between the serious dances.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the Kagyed dance at the Tsuklakhang?
faqs.a: Usually yes, as respectful spectators, though space in the courtyard is limited and access arrangements can vary. Arrive early, follow instructions from organisers and police, stay out of the dance area and avoid flash. Dress modestly and keep your voice low during the ritual.

faqs.q: Is Losoong the same as Losar?
faqs.a: No. Losoong is the Sikkimese Bhutia new year and harvest festival in December. Losar is the Tibetan new year, in February or March, celebrated by Tibetan and many Sikkimese Buddhist families and marked at monasteries such as Rumtek. Both involve masked dances beforehand, which can cause confusion.

name: Enchey Detor Chaam
when: Jan–Feb, 18th–19th days of the 12th Tibetan month (lunar)
community: Nyingma monastic community and Gangtok Buddhist families
summary: Each winter, the monks of Enchey Monastery above Gangtok perform the Detor Chaam, two days of masked dances in the courtyard on the 18th and 19th days of the 12th Tibetan month. It clears away obstacles before Losar and draws much of Gangtok up the hill.
body: Enchey, the Nyingma monastery on the ridge about 3 km above MG Marg, holds its annual Detor Chaam on the 18th and 19th days of the 12th month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in January or February, according to Wikipedia's article on the monastery. Like other Chaam, it is a ritual performed by monks to destroy negative forces before the new year, not a show for visitors.

Dancers in brocade robes and painted masks representing protector deities, including Mahakala, move slowly in the courtyard to drums, cymbals and long horns, while jesters break the solemnity. Enchey also performs the larger Singhe Chaam, the snow-lion dance, once every few years. Gangtok families come up the hill in their best clothes, often bringing children and elders, and sit in the same places each year.

Arrive by 9 am for a seat on the courtyard steps, bring a cushion and a warm layer, and stay behind the rope. Dates move with the lunar calendar every year; we confirm them in December. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Take a taxi up early; parking near the monastery is very limited on Chaam days.
Bring a cushion or mat for the stone steps and water for a long morning.
Ask before photographing families, and never step into the dance ground.

faqs.a: On the 18th and 19th days of the 12th Tibetan month, usually in January or February, according to Wikipedia's article on Enchey Monastery. The Gregorian dates change each year with the lunar calendar. We confirm them in December; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do we get to the Enchey Chaam?
faqs.a: Enchey is about 3 km from MG Marg, 10–15 minutes by taxi, at around ₹200–300 one way. On Chaam days traffic and parking on the ridge road are tight, so go early or walk up, which takes 50–60 minutes. Agree a pickup point with your driver for the return.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Enchey Chaam?
faqs.a: No ticket is normally charged; it is a religious festival open to the public. A small offering at the monastery is welcome. Organisers may restrict access to some areas, so follow their instructions, and stay behind the rope or line marking the dance ground.

faqs.q: Is the Enchey Chaam suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. Local families bring children, who usually enjoy the masks and the jesters. The crowd can be dense and the stone steps hard, so sit near an exit, bring snacks and water, and keep small children close. Some masks are fierce, which can frighten very young children.

name: Saga Dawa
when: May–Jun, full moon of the 4th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Saga Dawa marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing into parinirvana, celebrated on the full moon of the 4th Tibetan month, in May or June. In Gangtok, monks and devotees usually carry holy scriptures in a procession through the town, and the monasteries fill with butter lamps.
body: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year, and its full moon, the 15th day of the 4th month, commemorates three events in the life of the Buddha: his birth, his enlightenment and his passing. It corresponds to Vesak, celebrated across the Buddhist world, and in Sikkim it is a state holiday. Many families eat vegetarian food for the day or the month and make extra offerings and donations.

In Gangtok, the day usually brings a procession in which monks, accompanied by musicians and lay devotees, carry volumes of the scriptures through the streets of the town, and monasteries such as Enchey and the Tsuklakhang see a steady stream of visitors lighting butter lamps and turning prayer wheels. The atmosphere is devotional and calm rather than festive in the carnival sense.

Dates follow the lunar calendar and vary from year to year, usually falling in late May or June. Pre-monsoon showers are common by then, and haze often hides Kangchenjunga. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for the confirmed date and procession timing.
tips: Watch the procession from the roadside and step aside for the monks; do not cut through it.
Visit Enchey or the Do Drul Chorten in the evening to see butter lamps being lit.
Carry a light raincoat; Saga Dawa often falls with the first pre-monsoon showers.

faqs.q: When is Saga Dawa in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Saga Dawa falls on the full moon of the 4th Tibetan month, usually in late May or June. The exact date changes every year with the lunar calendar and appears on Sikkim's government holiday list once announced. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for the confirmed date.

faqs.q: What happens on Saga Dawa in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Monks and devotees usually carry holy scriptures in a procession through the town, accompanied by music, and the monasteries see many visitors lighting butter lamps and making offerings. Many Buddhist families eat vegetarian food on the day. It is a devotional day and a state holiday in Sikkim.

faqs.q: Is Saga Dawa the same as Buddha Purnima?
faqs.a: They mark the same occasion. Saga Dawa Düchen, on the full moon of the 4th Tibetan month, commemorates the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing, as Vesak and Buddha Purnima do elsewhere. Because Tibetan and Indian lunar calendars differ slightly, the dates do not always coincide.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Saga Dawa procession?
faqs.a: Visitors are welcome to watch respectfully from the roadside. Do not walk into or across the procession, keep a respectful distance from the monks carrying scriptures, and ask before photographing people at prayer. At monasteries, follow the usual etiquette: shoes off, walk clockwise and keep your voice low.
